title: Context and interpretation
keyIdea: Every text has two kinds of context. The context of production is the world it was made in: the writer's time, place, laws, beliefs and theatre. The context of reception is the time, place and values of each reader or audience. The words stay the same, but readers in different times and places bring different values, so they can read the same text in different ways. Good essays use context to sharpen an argument about the text, never to replace it.

kid: A play is written once, but it is read again and again. The world the writer lived in is the context of production. The time and place of the person reading or watching is the context of reception.

Take Katherine's last speech in The Taming of the Shrew. She tells wives to obey their husbands. The words have not changed since the 1590s. But audiences have. Around 1611 John Fletcher wrote a sequel where Petruchio is tamed himself. In 1929 Mary Pickford winked at the camera as she spoke the lines. Many modern stagings play the speech as irony, or as a woman worn down.
So meaning is not only in the words. It is made when a reader meets them. That does not mean any reading goes. You still need evidence from the text.

Use context to change how a line reads. Coverture meant a wife's goods became her husband's. So when Petruchio calls Kate 'my goods, my chattels', he is stating the law. That fact sharpens your point. A date you just drop in does not.
adult: A-level English Literature tests context directly. AQA, Edexcel and OCR all use Assessment Objective 3 for it. Students must show how the contexts in which texts are written and received shape meaning. Strong answers split the two. The context of production is the writer's era, genre, theatre, law and beliefs. The context of reception is any later audience, including the student.

The Taming of the Shrew is a classic test case. Within about 20 years, Fletcher's The Woman's Prize, or The Tamer Tamed, answered it. Garrick's 1754 version kept the taming as farce. The 1929 Pickford film added a wink. Modern stagings often unsettle the speech. Reception theory, from Jauss's horizon of expectations to reader-response criticism, explains why the same words yield new readings.

Common mistakes: bolting on facts about the writer's life that change nothing about a line. Presentism, which judges a 1590s text by a modern standard. Saying 'Elizabethans thought' as if a whole audience had one mind. And letting context replace close reading. A careful answer hedges with 'may have' or 'some audiences', ties each fact to a quotation, and keeps the text at the centre.

In the lab your teenager sorts six contexts into production or reception. Next they place four real responses to Katherine's speech on a timeline. Then they judge whether context sentences sharpen a point or are bolted on. Finally they match one line to historicist, feminist and performance readings, and catch the classic slips.

familyTip: Watch two short clips of the same scene from different productions or films together and ask: what did each director want the audience to feel, and what about their own time might explain the choice?

visual.caption: Is each one a context of production or of reception? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: split production and reception, date four audiences, judge context use, match lenses, spot slips.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a context of production for The Taming of the Shrew?
choices: Women's roles were played by boy actors
A modern audience's views on control in relationships
A film version made in 1929
practice.hint: Production is the world the play was first made and staged in.
practice.explain: Boy actors playing women belongs to how the play was first made and staged in the 1590s, so it is production. The other two are later audiences: reception.

practice.prompt: A reader in {y} finds Katherine's final speech disturbing. Which context mainly explains this?
choices: The context of reception
The context of production
The play's source material
practice.hint: Whose world is shaping the response: the writer's or the reader's?
practice.explain: A reaction in {y} comes from that reader's own values and time, which is the context of reception.

practice.prompt: Which sentence uses context to sharpen an argument?
choices: Under coverture a wife's goods became her husband's, so 'my goods, my chattels' states the law, not just a boast
Shakespeare was born in Stratford in 1564
The Elizabethan era was a time of great change
practice.hint: Which one changes how you read a specific line?
practice.explain: The coverture sentence ties a fact to a quotation and changes how we read it. The others are true or vague but change nothing about the play.

practice.prompt: Fletcher answered the play in a sequel about {n} years after it was written. What does that show?
choices: Early audiences did not all accept the taming
Fletcher misunderstood Shakespeare
The play was forgotten until the 20th century
practice.hint: If someone writes a reply, did everyone agree with the original?
practice.explain: A sequel in which Petruchio is tamed, written only about {n} years later, shows the taming was argued with in its own era. So a resistant reading is not purely modern.

pool.prompt: What is the context of reception?
choices: The time, place and values of whoever reads or watches the text
The time and place where the author wrote it
The plot events that come before a scene
pool.hint: Reception means receiving: who is receiving the text?
pool.explain: The context of reception is the time, place and values of the reader or audience, at any point. The author's world is the context of production.

pool.prompt: 'Shakespeare was sexist because he did not support votes for women.' What is the slip?
choices: Presentism: judging the past by a modern standard
It uses too much evidence
It confuses comedy with tragedy
pool.hint: When did campaigns for women's votes begin?
pool.explain: Votes for women were not a live issue in the 1590s, so this judges the past by a much later standard. That slip is called presentism.

pool.prompt: Why is 'Elizabethan audiences found the ending funny' a weak claim?
choices: It treats a whole audience as having one reaction
Elizabethans never watched comedies
The ending is not in the play
pool.hint: Did every person in the theatre react the same way?
pool.explain: It assumes one audience mind. Hedge it: 'some original audiences may have laughed', especially as Fletcher's sequel shows others resisted.

pool.prompt: Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea retells Jane Eyre from Bertha's point of view. It is best described as...
choices: a later reinterpretation shaped by its own context
proof of what Charlotte Brontë intended
the context of production of Jane Eyre
pool.hint: It was written in 1966, over a century after Jane Eyre.
pool.explain: Written in 1966, it reads Jane Eyre from a postcolonial position. That makes it a reception, not evidence of Brontë's intent.

pool.prompt: In a {n}-mark essay, what should context do?
choices: Sharpen an argument about the text
Replace close reading of quotations
Fill the first paragraph with background
pool.hint: Examiners reward context that is linked to the text.
pool.explain: In a {n}-mark essay, context earns credit when it changes how a line or choice is read. It supports close reading and never replaces it.

pool.prompt: A director in {y} stages Katherine's speech as bitter irony. What does this show?
choices: Reception can reshape how a text's meaning is presented
The words of the speech were rewritten
The play has no meaning of its own
pool.hint: The words are the same. What changed?
pool.explain: The {y} staging keeps the words but changes delivery and framing. That shows reception shaping meaning, while the text still limits what is plausible.

pool.prompt: Reading 'Thy husband is thy lord' against the 1563 Homily on matrimony is which kind of reading?
choices: Historicist
Performance-based
Purely personal response
pool.hint: It reads the line beside a document from the same era.
pool.explain: Setting the line beside a document from its own time is a historicist reading of the context of production.
